paragraphs.source_en: In this section the potential functions of painted sites are examined. Jelinek (1980) states that at Sefar and in other sites with complex compositions the high level of symbolism in paintings suggests that these sites were not inhabited but that they served for spiritual purposes. In the attempt to reconstruct the possible functions of painted sites and/or shelters I present some examples from the ethnography of African populations who use shelters for different purposes. Places and natural features are fundamental elements in all African religion and African people all over the continent are reported to have sacred stones and rocks, which are used for religious rites and they are often employed in rainmaking ceremonies (Mbiti 1969). Many consider rocks, boulders and caves to be the dwelling places of the spirits or the living dead.

units.source_en: Ethnographic records from Africa indicate that certain localities and shelters had a special function and importance for a local group or for numerous groups living in the area (Lee 1979; Goodman 1988).
The main difference is between vast places accessible to a large community, and between smaller sites or single shelters designated as allowed to only some individuals.
The places can thus be divided into two main groups:

paragraphs.source_en: - z places of inter-regional importance (for many groups or a large community) - z places of regional or local importance (for a single group or a few groups).

paragraphs.source_en: The places accessible and designated to a large community are those of periodical meetings of groups living in the same larger area. Such meetings are best documented from the ! Kung hunter-gatherers in South Africa (Lee&De Vore 1976; Lee1979). Among the ! Kung, within a territory, the water hole and the area immediately around it is owned by the group, and this ownership is passed from one generation to another as long as the descendants continue to live there. This core area is surrounded by a broad belt of land that is shared with adjacent groups. The most common pattern, documented also for other hunter-gatherers such as Pygmies, Arctic Indians, Great Basin Indians and North West Coast Indians, is the seasonal concentration and dispersion of groups (Lee 1979).
